paragraphs: For most of the twentieth century, the suppression of side shoots by a growing tip, known as apical dominance, was explained by a single hormone. Auxin, made in the young leaves of the shoot apex and carried downward through the stem, was held to inhibit the buds in the axils of older leaves directly: cut off the tip, and the flow of auxin ceased, releasing the buds. The account had the virtue of economy, and decapitation experiments seemed to make its truth palpable, since auxin paste smeared on the cut stump kept the buds below it from growing. Its difficulty was that auxin applied directly to a bud seldom stopped the bud from growing, and radiolabeled auxin moving down the stem was found scarcely to enter the buds at all.

Two revisions followed, and they are often presented as rivals. One holds that auxin acts at a distance by regulating a second signal, the strigolactones (compounds first known as the cues by which parasitic weeds detect a host's roots), which moves up into the buds and does the inhibiting. The other holds that a bud grows only if it can export its own auxin into the stem, so that the main stem's auxin stream suppresses buds simply by occupying the transport channels a bud would need. Yet the two accounts need not exclude each other: strigolactones have been shown to dampen auxin transport itself, which suggests that the second signal may mediate dominance partly by narrowing the very channels the competition model describes. What neither revision easily explains is timing. In decapitated pea plants, buds begin to swell within hours, before any change in auxin level could have traveled down the stem to reach them; what does arrive that quickly is sugar, diverted from the lost apex. That observation does not oust auxin from the story, since sustained outgrowth still depends on it, but it does portend a model in which the hormone governs whether released buds persist rather than whether they are released at all.

Critics have long been embarrassed by apostrophe, the ode's habit of addressing winds, urns and birds as though they could listen. To a generation trained to prize irony, the 'O' that opens so many Romantic odes sounded like a relic of rhetoric-book enthusiasm, and the most influential mid-century readings treated it as scaffolding the poem had to climb past before its real, pensive work could begin. A later school reversed the valuation, arguing that the address is the ode's real work: by calling on a thing as if it were a person, the poet tries to make the world answer, and the poem limns the failure of that attempt as fully as its hope. This account has the merit of taking the odes at their word, though its proponents sometimes write as if every apostrophe were a metaphysical crisis. Many of the period's odes, especially the comic and occasional ones that critics rarely read, use the vocative with irreverent ease, hailing a teapot or a fashionable hat with no expectation of a reply. A history of the form that included them might find that the numinous address was one possibility among several rather than the essence of the genre.

Eighteen months ago the Corvan hotel chain replaced the paper comment cards in its guest rooms with a short survey e-mailed to every guest after checkout. Since the change, the share of responses rating the stay as poor has fallen from 14 percent to 6 percent. The chain's operations director concludes that the quality of service at Corvan hotels has improved over the period.

It was long a commonplace that the printing press, by multiplying identical copies, called a new reading public into being and fixed texts in a stable form for the first time. The commonplace has been battered from two directions. Bibliographers have shown that early printed books were anything but identical: compositors corrected proofs while the press was running, so that sheets from the same edition differ, and pirated reprints introduced errors faster than authorized editions could remove them. Textual stability, on this view, was not a property of the technology but an achievement of later institutions, such as copyright, learned editing and the reputations of particular firms, that made some printed versions authoritative. Economic historians, meanwhile, have pointed out that the printers of the first half-century depended for their survival on a clientele that already existed: clergy, lawyers and university men who bought Latin breviaries, legal commentaries and school grammars. Printers who gambled on new kinds of readers often went bankrupt; the pecuniary logic of the trade pushed them toward the tried and saleable.

The second correction, however, does not quite dispose of the claim it targets. The paradigmatic product of the early press, measured by the number of copies rather than of titles, was not the folio Bible but the single sheet: indulgence certificates, printed by the tens of thousands; broadsides announcing edicts; almanacs; and, from the 1520s, the pamphlets of a factious religious controversy in which each side lambasted the other in the vernacular. Such ephemera survive poorly, which is why catalogs organized by title understate them. They did not address an existing clientele; they found readers in the propinquity of market and parish, among people who might own no book at all but who read, or heard read, a sheet nailed to a church door. If print created a new public, it did so less through the books historians have counted than through the paper they have mostly lost.

Offered $100 today or $110 in a week, many people take the $100; offered $100 in a year or $110 in a year and a week, most will wait for the larger sum. This reversal, impatience about the near term combined with patience about the distant one, has been taken as the signature of present bias, a tendency to weight the immediate moment more heavily than any constant rate of discounting would allow, and it is routinely invoked to explain why people who sincerely resolve to save or to exercise do neither when the moment arrives, apparently oblivious to the inconstancy their own past choices might have taught them to expect.

The inference is less secure than it looks. Money is fungible: a subject who seems insouciant about the extra $10 may simply bank the $100, so a choice between sums reveals little about when anything will be consumed. Nor does the reversal by itself nullify the subject's claim to rationality. A subject unsure whether the experimenter will pay at all has reason to treat any delay as a risk, and reason to expect that, if a year passes without default, she will trust the experimenter more; a week's wait that begins a year hence is thus one she expects to face with greater confidence, and her impatience about the present need betray no failure of will.

The strongest evidence for present bias has accordingly come from studies that remove both confounds by offering subjects not money but work: units of a tedious task to be completed on one date or another, which cannot be banked and whose completion no experimenter can jeopardize by defaulting. Subjects asked weeks ahead to divide the work between two dates tend to choose an even split; when the first date arrives and they are invited to revise, many push a substantial share to the later one. Present bias survives the critique, then, but its natural home is the scheduling of effort, and the habit of measuring it in dollars may have flattered the theory with evidence it had not earned.

In the head of a sunflower, the florets lie along two families of spirals, one winding clockwise and one counterclockwise, and the number of spirals in each family is almost always a pair of consecutive Fibonacci numbers such as 34 and 55. Since the polymath naturalists of the nineteenth century first tabulated such counts, the regularity has invited explanations from optimality: the angle between successive organs, close to 137.5 degrees, was said to have been favored because it packs florets most densely or spaces leaves so that none shades another. Experiments on the growing tip have since favored a mechanism that makes no reference to such benefits. On this account, each new organ begins as a primordial swelling where a growth-promoting hormone is most concentrated, and each, once formed, draws the hormone toward itself, depleting the surrounding tissue and so demarcating a zone in which no neighbor can arise. Computer models built on nothing more than this rule of mutual inhibition reproduce both the divergence angle and the Fibonacci spirals, though no one programs either into them. This does not show that the arrangement confers no advantage; a pattern generated by a simple mechanism may still have been retained because it proved useful. It does show that the pattern's regularity is no evidence of such an advantage, since a mechanism indifferent to efficiency would produce the regularity anyway. Nor is the pattern quite the nonpareil it is sometimes made out to be: in many species, and in sunflowers grown under stress, non-Fibonacci counts turn up at rates that the inhibition models, once a little random noise is added, predict rather well.

In the province of Vastra, restaurants are inspected at unannounced times, and any inspection that finds a serious violation triggers a follow-up visit within thirty days, at which an uncorrected violation brings a heavy fine. Five years ago that fine was doubled. Since then, the proportion of follow-up visits finding the original violation uncorrected has fallen steadily, while the proportion of first inspections finding a serious violation has remained about the same. The standards inspectors use to classify a violation as serious have not changed over the period.

questions.prompt: Those who had called the commission ___ were not wrong about the calendar, since its report arrived fourteen months after the deadline; they had simply mistaken the cause, for the delay owed nothing to the commissioners' habits and everything to a ministry that released its files a few pages at a time.

explanation.key: The critics were 'right about the calendar' (the report was late) but wrong about the cause, which they had located in 'the commissioners' habits'. So the charge was that the commissioners were habitually slow to act: dilatory.

distractors.precipitate: A timing word, but the opposite one: the report was late, not hasty.
distractors.complaisant: Overly eager to please; the ministry is mentioned, but the charge the calendar bears on is slowness, not deference.
distractors.austere: Severe or plain; nothing about the calendar bears on it.
distractors.caustic: Biting in tone; a lateness charge is not about tone.

questions.prompt: Campaigners who had braced for hostility met something harder to answer: (i) ___ so thorough that even their most (ii) ___ appeals, from megaphones at the station to slogans painted across the bridge, drew not jeers but shrugs.

explanation.key: (i) They braced for hostility and met 'instead' something else; the shrugs show indifference: apathy. (ii) Megaphones and painted slogans are loud, insistent appeals: strident.

distractors.animus: Hostility is what they braced for and did not get; jeers, not shrugs, would show it.
distractors.diffuse: Wordy or unfocused; slogans and megaphones are pointed and loud.

questions.prompt: The editor's introduction was (i) ___ to a fault: she claimed only to have transcribed the poet's notebooks, not to have interpreted them. The claim was less innocent than it sounded, since a transcriber who refuses to count the poet's erratic spelling among the (ii) ___ worth preserving, and treats it instead as matter (iii) ___ to the poems, to be silently corrected, has already interpreted a great deal.

explanation.key: (i) Claiming 'only' to have transcribed, and the claim sounding 'innocent', marks an unassuming introduction: modest. (ii) The spelling is erratic and the poet's own, so the things 'worth preserving' it is refused a place among are personal peculiarities: idiosyncrasies. (iii) Matter to be silently corrected is treated as not belonging to the poems: extraneous.

distractors.grandiloquent: Pompous; the opposite of claiming only to transcribe.
distractors.tendentious: Promoting a cause; that is what the author goes on to suspect, not what the introduction appeared to be ('sounded innocent').
distractors.conventions: Erratic spelling is by definition not conventional.
distractors.excrescences: Ugly outgrowths are not things 'worth preserving'; the word describes how the editor treats the spelling, not what she refuses to see it as.
distractors.integral: The opposite: treating the spelling as integral would mean keeping it.
distractors.endemic: Native to; matter endemic to the poems would belong to them, which contradicts silently correcting it.

questions.prompt: Auditors had flagged each of the clerk's shortcuts and dismissed each as trivial, which was precisely what made the practice so ___: no single entry ever looked worth correcting, and by the time the accounts were reconciled the errors had compounded beyond easy repair.
choices: flagrant
pernicious
venial
inconsequential
insidious
egregious

explanation.key: Harm that grows unnoticed because each step looks trivial is subtle, gradual harm: pernicious and insidious.

distractors.flagrant: Trap pair with 'egregious': both mean conspicuously bad, but the point is that no entry looked bad at all.
distractors.venial: Minor and forgivable; describes each shortcut as the auditors saw it, not the practice whose errors compounded. Pairs in meaning with 'inconsequential', both wrong.

questions.prompt: The biographer's portrait of the composer as ___ rests largely on the testimony of his copyists, who bore the brunt of his tirades; his pupils, whom he never once rebuked, remembered a different man.
choices: irascible
taciturn
benevolent
choleric
reticent
magnanimous

explanation.key: The portrait rests on witnesses to his tirades, and the pupils who were never rebuked saw 'a different man': the portrait is of a quick-tempered man, irascible and choleric.

distractors.taciturn: Trap pair with 'reticent': both mean disinclined to speak, which tirades contradict.
distractors.benevolent: Trap pair with 'magnanimous': this is the pupils' 'different man', not the biographer's portrait.

questions.prompt: Critics who predicted that the reform would merely ___ the harshness of the old sentencing code, leaving its machinery intact, were proved right in a way they had not foreseen: sentences on paper grew shorter, but because early parole was abolished at the same stroke, the time prisoners actually served scarcely changed.
choices: exacerbate
temper
codify
aggravate
mitigate
abrogate

explanation.key: The prediction came true in an unforeseen way: sentences 'on paper grew shorter', so the reform did soften the code's harshness, though only nominally. Temper (secondary sense, to moderate) and mitigate both mean to make less severe.

distractors.exacerbate: Trap pair with 'aggravate': the unchanged time served might suggest harshness stayed or rose, but the prediction that proved right is about shorter sentences, a softening.
distractors.codify: To set down systematically; shorter sentences do not confirm a prediction of codification.
distractors.abrogate: To abolish formally; abolishing the harshness clashes with 'merely' and with 'leaving its machinery intact'.

questions.prompt: Though her dispatches ran to dozens of pages, the ambassador was so ___ that historians have had to reconstruct her views chiefly from what she conspicuously declined to report.
choices: terse
discreet
candid
laconic
circumspect
prolix

explanation.key: Writing at length while withholding what she thought means careful reserve, not brevity: discreet and circumspect.

distractors.terse: Trap pair with 'laconic': both mean brief, which fits withholding but is ruled out by 'Though her dispatches ran to dozens of pages'.
distractors.candid: The opposite: candor would leave nothing to reconstruct.
distractors.prolix: Fits the dozens of pages, but 'Though' sets the blank against length, and wordiness does not explain reconstructing views from omissions.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes the organization of the passage?
choices: A long-standing explanation is defended against two objections, and an observation is then cited that confirms it.
A long-standing explanation is described and refuted; two successor accounts are compared and one is shown to be superior; and an observation is cited that confirms the superior account.

A long-standing explanation is described along with evidence against it; two successor accounts are presented and partly reconciled; and an observation is cited that limits the role of a factor all of these accounts share.
A long-standing explanation is described along with evidence against it; two successor accounts are presented as incompatible alternatives; and an observation is cited that decides between them.
Two rival accounts of a phenomenon are presented, an older account is shown to combine them, and an observation is cited that eliminates the factor the older account relied on.

explanation.key: Paragraph 1: the direct-inhibition account and the evidence against it (auxin on buds, labeled auxin not entering). Paragraph 2: two revisions, 'often presented as rivals' but said to 'need not exclude each other'; then the timing observation, which 'does not oust auxin' but restricts it to governing persistence. Auxin is common to all three accounts.

distractors.A long-standing explanation is defended: The older account is undermined, not defended.
distractors.A long-standing explanation is described: Neither revision is preferred; the timing observation troubles both.
One move off: the author says the revisions 'need not exclude each other', and the sugar observation decides between neither.
distractors.Two rival accounts of a phenomenon are p: Wrong order, and too strong: the observation 'does not oust auxin'.

questions.prompt: Consider each of the choices separately and select all that apply. The passage suggests which of the following about the experiments in which auxin paste was applied to the cut stump?
choices: Their results are consistent with the view that auxin suppresses buds without entering them.
They were later found to have used auxin at concentrations far higher than those that occur in an intact stem.
Their results could not by themselves distinguish the strigolactone account from the account in which a bud must export its own auxin.

explanation.key: A: yes. The paste kept buds dormant, yet labeled auxin 'scarcely' enters buds; the result fits action at a distance, which is what both revisions propose. B: no. A familiar historical criticism, but the passage never mentions concentrations; the paste experiments are said only to have 'seemed' to confirm the old account. C: yes. Both revisions predict that auxin flowing down from the stump keeps buds suppressed (by inducing the second signal, or by occupying the transport channels), so the result cannot favor either.

questions.prompt: The author's attitude toward the 'later school' of critics is best described as
choices: enthusiastic endorsement, tempered only by regret that they discarded the mid-century readings
qualified approval: the author credits them with taking the odes seriously but doubts that their account holds for the genre as a whole
respectful disagreement: the author accepts their interest in apostrophe but rejects their claim that the odes record the failure of address
scorn: the author regards their reading as a revival of the rhetoric-book enthusiasm that earlier critics deplored
neutrality: the author reports their position without evaluating it

explanation.key: The author grants 'the merit of taking the odes at their word' but faults the school for treating 'every apostrophe' as a crisis, and argues that comic and occasional odes make that address 'one possibility among several'.

distractors.enthusiastic endorsement, tempered only: Too strong, and the author never regrets the loss of the mid-century view.
distractors.respectful disagreement: the author acce: Half-right: the author does not dispute the failure reading for the odes it fits; the objection is to its scope.
distractors.scorn: the author regards their reading: Too strong, and the link to rhetoric-book enthusiasm is the mid-century critics' charge against the poems.
distractors.neutrality: the author reports their pos: The author plainly evaluates it ('has the merit', 'sometimes write as if').

questions.prompt: Select the sentence that states what, according to the later school, the poet attempts to accomplish by addressing a thing as a person.

explanation.key: The third sentence ('A later school reversed the valuation...') says that by calling on a thing as if it were a person 'the poet tries to make the world answer'. The fifth sentence reuses the idea of a reply ('no expectation of a reply'), but it describes comic odes, not the later school's account.

questions.prompt: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the director's conclusion?
choices: The number of survey responses received each month is now several times the number of comment cards that guests formerly returned.
Guests who were satisfied with their stay seldom bothered to fill out a comment card, whereas the e-mailed survey is answered by a broad cross-section of guests.
Over the same period, the number of complaints made in person to front-desk staff at Corvan hotels has also declined.
Some guests who receive the e-mailed survey delete it without opening it.
During the period, Corvan raised its room rates at most of its hotels.

explanation.key: The argument assumes the two measures sample guests alike. If cards came mostly from unhappy guests and the survey from everyone, the share of poor ratings would fall even with no change in service.

distractors.The number of survey responses received: More responses alone say nothing about who responds; the share could fall or rise.
distractors.Some guests who receive the e-mailed sur: Non-response with no stated direction; cards had non-response too.
distractors.During the period, Corvan raised its roo: Higher prices would if anything raise expectations and poor ratings, so it does not explain the decline.

questions.prompt: The foundation's grants were famously generous, and its directors ___ only where outsiders least expected: on the salaries of the scientists whose work they paid for, reasoning that instruments would outlast any single career.

explanation.key: Generous everywhere 'only' except salaries, with money steered toward instruments instead: they were sparing on salaries, i.e. they stinted (secondary sense: to skimp). The noun 'stint' (a period of service, echoed by 'any single career') is the everyday sense.

distractors.lavished: Trap pair with 'splurged': the generosity was everywhere else, and the reasoning about instruments shows salaries were where they held back.
distractors.temporized: To stall for time; nothing about delay.
distractors.acceded: To agree to a demand; the reasoning clause describes a choice to spend elsewhere, not a concession.

questions.prompt: That the two governments announced the treaty in nearly identical language seemed to (i) ___ the rumors of discord between them; in fact, each foreign ministry had chosen the wording precisely because, read against each country's constitution, the same phrase committed the two governments to principles (ii) ___ to each other.

explanation.key: (i) Identical language looks like harmony, so it 'seemed to' contradict the rumors: belie (to show to be false). (ii) 'In fact' reverses that appearance, so the discord was real: the shared phrase hid principles directly opposed to each other, antithetical.

distractors.corroborate: The opposite: identical language would seem to refute, not confirm, rumors of discord.
distractors.occasion: To cause; identical wording would not seem to produce rumors of discord.
distractors.akin: Kindred principles are the harmony that 'in fact' was meant to reverse.
distractors.ancillary: Subordinate or supporting principles imply cooperation, not the hidden discord 'in fact' reveals.

questions.prompt: The (i) ___ that greeted the senator's vote came, oddly, less from her opponents, who were too pleased that she had at last (ii) ___ to begrudge her the delay, than from allies who could have forgiven her for declining to oppose the bill (had she simply chosen to (iii) ___) but not for lending it her name.

explanation.key: (i) Allies who could not forgive her 'lending it her name' supplied harsh public censure: opprobrium. (ii) Opponents were pleased she had 'at last' come over to their bill after a 'delay': she capitulated. (iii) Declining to oppose without supporting means not voting at all: abstain.

distractors.acclaim: Praise; it would not come chiefly from unforgiving allies.
distractors.equanimity: Calm; contradicts the allies' refusal to forgive.
distractors.stonewalled: Continued resistance; opponents would not be pleased by it, and she did vote for the bill.
distractors.equivocated: Hedging; she lent the bill her name, a definite act.
distractors.acquiesce: To comply is what she actually did (voting yes), which the allies could not forgive.
distractors.concur: Agreeing with the bill is the act the allies objected to, not the alternative they would have forgiven.

questions.prompt: Students who expected the critic's books to be as (i) ___ as his lectures, which audiences left half-humming his cadences, found instead (ii) ___ catalogs of variant readings, footnoted to the comma; yet the dryness was principled, for he distrusted any claim about a poem that could not be checked against (iii) ___ evidence, such as the surviving manuscripts and printings.

explanation.key: (i) Audiences left 'half-humming his cadences': sweet-sounding, mellifluous. (ii) Dry catalogs 'footnoted to the comma' are excessively concerned with minute detail: pedantic. (iii) Evidence one can check, such as manuscripts and printings, is observational: empirical.

distractors.acerbic: Sharp in tone; not what makes lectures hummable.
distractors.polemical: Combative; catalogs of variants footnoted to the comma are fussy, not argumentative.
distractors.intuitive: Manuscripts and printings are not intuitions.

questions.prompt: The reviewer's praise for the novel's 'remarkably familiar' plot was her way of contriving to ___, without exposing herself to a suit for libel, what she could never have printed in plain words: that the author had lifted the story from an older book.
choices: proclaim
intimate
refute
declare
insinuate
concede

explanation.key: Saying something through ambiguous praise rather than 'in plain words' is hinting: intimate (secondary sense, to suggest indirectly) and insinuate. The 'familiar' in the sentence baits the everyday adjective sense of 'intimate'.

distractors.refute: She was suggesting the plagiarism, not disproving it.
distractors.concede: Conceding implies granting a point under pressure; she was the one advancing the charge.
distractors.proclaim: Trap pair with 'declare': both mean to announce openly, the very thing she 'could never have printed in plain words' and that would expose her to a libel suit.

questions.prompt: Vendors had long read the council's decade of silence as tacit acceptance of their unlicensed market, so its vote to ___ the market startled them, not because the vote reversed that acceptance but because it made it official, complete with permits, a fee schedule and a municipal seal.
choices: penalize
sanction
overlook
censure
endorse
disparage

explanation.key: The vote did not reverse acceptance but 'made it official': formal approval, sanction (secondary sense, to authorize) and endorse.

distractors.penalize: Trap pair with 'censure': a vote against the market would startle, but the sentence says the vote did not reverse the acceptance. 'Penalize' is also the everyday sense of 'sanction'.
distractors.overlook: Ignoring the market is the tacit acceptance that already existed, not an official act.
distractors.disparage: Belittling contradicts making the market official.

questions.prompt: Historians who dated the town's feud to the riot of 1911 mistook its first eruption for its origin: the grievances behind it had lain ___ for a generation, surfacing only in the dry language of boundary suits before anyone thought to take up arms.
choices: manifest
latent
evanescent
patent
dormant
nominal

explanation.key: The riot was the 'first eruption', not the 'origin', so the grievances existed long before without breaking out: latent and dormant.

distractors.manifest: Trap pair with 'patent': both mean obvious, but grievances visible only in dry legal language were exactly what the historians missed.
distractors.nominal: In name only; the grievances were real enough to cause a feud.

questions.prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: defend a familiar claim about early printing against critics who have misread the evidence
argue that a familiar claim about early printing, though rightly criticized in some respects, retains some validity for reasons its critics have overlooked
show that the critics of a familiar claim about early printing have relied on a misleading kind of evidence
explain why early printers preferred established customers to new kinds of readers
reconcile two competing critiques of a familiar claim about early printing

explanation.key: The author lets the bibliographers' critique of textual fixity stand, accepts the economic historians' account of books, and then argues that the 'new public' part of the claim survives through single-sheet ephemera the critics did not count.

distractors.defend a familiar claim about early prin: Wrong verb: the author accepts most of the criticism.
distractors.show that the critics of a familiar clai: Half-right: title catalogs do understate ephemera, but that bears only on the second critique, and the bibliographers' critique is left standing.
distractors.explain why early printers preferred est: Too narrow: a point from the first paragraph.
distractors.reconcile two competing critiques of a f: The critiques do not compete; they come 'from two directions' against the same claim.

questions.prompt: The passage most strongly suggests which of the following?
choices: Printers of single sheets were less likely than printers of books to go bankrupt.
Most people in the early sixteenth century who encountered printed matter owned no books.
The economic historians' picture of the early trade may have been shaped partly by which printed materials happened to survive.
Vernacular pamphlets outnumbered Latin books, in copies printed, from the beginning of printing.
The variations among sheets that bibliographers found in printed books were even more common in printed ephemera.

explanation.key: The economic historians describe a trade serving an existing clientele of book buyers (paragraph 1). Paragraph 2 says ephemera, which reached new readers, 'survive poorly' and are understated in title catalogs, and that historians counted books while losing the paper. Together: their picture may reflect survival.

distractors.Printers of single sheets were less like: Plausible, but the passage says nothing about bankruptcy among sheet printers.
distractors.Most people in the early sixteenth centu: Too strong: the passage says such readers 'might own no book at all', not that most did not.
distractors.Vernacular pamphlets outnumbered Latin b: The pamphlets date 'from the 1520s', not the beginning, and the single sheet as a class is what dominated.
distractors.The variations among sheets that bibliog: Unsupported; ephemera are not discussed in connection with textual variation.

questions.prompt: Consider each of the choices separately and select all that apply. The passage supports which of the following statements about the single-sheet products of the early press?
choices: Catalogs that count titles give a misleading impression of how large a share of the press's output they made up.
Most of them were commissioned by church or civil authorities rather than printed on the printers' own speculation.
They could reach readers who had not bought them.

explanation.key: A: yes. Measured by copies they were the 'paradigmatic product', yet 'catalogs organized by title understate them'. B: no. Indulgences and edicts were issued by authorities, but the list also includes almanacs and controversial pamphlets, and the passage gives no proportions, so 'most' is unsupported. C: yes. People who owned no book read a sheet 'nailed to a church door', so a sheet could be read without being bought.

questions.prompt: In the context in which it appears, 'flattered' most nearly means
choices: praised insincerely
gratified
made to seem better supported than it was
imitated approvingly
exaggerated the popularity of

explanation.key: Measuring in dollars supplied 'evidence it had not earned': it made the theory look stronger than the evidence warranted.

distractors.praised insincerely: The everyday sense; no one is praising the theory.
distractors.gratified: Pleasing someone; a theory cannot be pleased.
distractors.exaggerated the popularity of: The issue is evidential support, not how widely the theory is held.

questions.prompt: Which of the following findings would the author most likely regard as the clearest evidence of present bias?
choices: Shoppers offered a $20 store credit today or a $25 credit next month, both redeemable for cash, mostly take the $20 credit.
Investors whose repayment is guaranteed by a government insurer still prefer a smaller payment now to a larger one in a year.
Volunteers who in January sign up to spend equal numbers of hours sorting donations in March and in April, and whose stipend has already been paid, ask in March to move most of their hours to April.
Diners offered a dessert today or a larger dessert next week, at a restaurant that has twice canceled reservations without notice, choose today's dessert.
Employees who prefer a larger bonus in two years to a smaller one in one year also prefer a larger bonus in one year to a smaller one now.

explanation.key: The author accepts evidence that removes both confounds: the good must be something that cannot be banked (effort), no one's promise may be at risk (stipend already paid), and the choice must reverse as the date nears. The volunteers meet all three.

distractors.Shoppers offered a $20 store credit toda: Cash-redeemable credit is fungible, the store's promise is at risk, and there is no reversal.
distractors.Investors whose repayment is guaranteed: Removes the trust confound only; money is still fungible, and no reversal is shown.
distractors.Diners offered a dessert today or a larg: Surface match (a non-monetary good), but the restaurant's unreliability makes impatience rational on the author's own argument.
distractors.Employees who prefer a larger bonus in t: Consistent patience, the opposite of the reversal that signals present bias.

questions.prompt: Select the sentence that reports the finding on which the author's claim that the spirals' regularity is no evidence of an advantage most directly depends.

explanation.key: The fifth sentence ('Computer models built on nothing more than this rule of mutual inhibition reproduce both the divergence angle and the Fibonacci spirals...') is the finding that shows a mechanism indifferent to efficiency does produce the regularity, which is the 'since' clause of the seventh sentence. The third sentence only reports that experiments favored such a mechanism. The fourth ('On this account...') states the hypothesized mechanism; it is not a finding and does not show that the mechanism yields the spirals. The sixth is a concession, not evidence.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes the organization of the passage?
choices: A pattern is described; an explanation from its supposed benefits is reported; a mechanism is presented that produces the pattern without reference to benefits; the bearing of that mechanism on the earlier explanation is limited; and a common characterization of the pattern is qualified.
A pattern is described; two explanations of it are contrasted; and the older explanation is shown to be false.
A pattern is described; a mechanism is presented that produces it; the mechanism's implications are limited; and evidence is offered that the explanation from benefits is correct after all.
A pattern is described; a mechanism that produces it is presented; and an explanation from the pattern's benefits is then introduced as a more complete account.
A pattern is described; an explanation from its supposed benefits is reported; a mechanism is presented that confirms that explanation; and exceptions to the pattern are dismissed as noise.

explanation.key: Spirals described; optimality explanation reported; mutual-inhibition mechanism presented; 'This does not show...' / 'It does show...' limit what follows for optimality; 'Nor is the pattern quite the nonpareil' qualifies its supposed uniformity.

distractors.A pattern is described; two explanations: Too strong: the author says the arrangement may still confer an advantage.
distractors.A pattern is described; a mechanism is p: Skips the optimality explanation's introduction, and the ending offers no such evidence.
distractors.A pattern is described; a mechanism that: Order reversed: the optimality explanation comes first and is the one undercut.
distractors.A pattern is described; an explanation f: The mechanism 'makes no reference to such benefits', and the exceptions are predicted by the models, not dismissed.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is most strongly supported by the statements above?
choices: The doubling of the fine caused the decline in the proportion of uncorrected violations found at follow-up visits.
Whatever has made restaurants more likely to correct serious violations has not made them less likely to commit such violations in the first place.
Most restaurants found to have a serious violation now correct it before the follow-up visit.
Inspectors have become less thorough at follow-up visits than they were five years ago.
Restaurants in Vastra commit fewer serious violations than restaurants in provinces that do not conduct follow-up visits.

explanation.key: Uncorrected violations at follow-up fell, while serious violations found at first inspection held steady under unchanged standards. So whatever drove more correcting did not reduce committing.

distractors.The doubling of the fine caused the decl: Timing alone does not establish cause; other factors could explain the decline.
distractors.Most restaurants found to have a serious: The proportion fell, but no figure shows it is below half.
distractors.Inspectors have become less thorough at: One possible explanation of the decline, but nothing in the statements supports it.
